original:
So inner child therapy draws on those higher vantage points more concretely. The inner Guide is the closest thing here to a Higher Self, and it has to work with the Nurturer and Protector and come after them. It can’t act like some transcendent authority that waves everything away. Most reparenting doesn’t do enough with the Guide, which is the opposite extreme from IFS, so I’m trying to bring together the best of both. IFS isn’t exactly one system, so I may be simplifying it here. It has its own branches and disputes, and that’s one more problem I’m trying to remedy by laying all this out systematically in this guide.
IFS calls these wounded young parts “exiles.” I find that pathologizing. I prefer to speak of a child who needs parenting and integration, rather than naming them by their wounded or excluded condition.
And the parts just keep coming: managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts... At some point it’s a maze, with a little one somewhere in the middle of it. Some practitioners are gentle about it and walk you through the maze just fine. Others seem to leave people more split up than when they started. A big institute and a pile of certificates won’t tell you whether a model is true, or whether it’s safe for you.

original: In one of the Buddha’s own accounts of how he woke up, ill will shows up in his mind and he sees it’s hurting him. If he had to figure that out by watching, it’s not obvious. Ill will can make you feel powerful. Being on fire would too, and people would definitely get out of your way, but unless you’re the Human Torch from the Fantastic Four, you’d be the one burning. Has it ever left anybody at ease, with nothing to regret afterward?

original:
Borrow One Competency at a Time
A complete ideal parent may be impossible to imagine (unless you saw The Brady Bunch). And imagination is pretty hard for adults anyway since it kinda gets stamped out of kids at an early age, but it’s not just a foolish waste of time. It’s actually a genius mode unlock. So since the adult is actually a baby when it comes to power to imagine, start small: Borrow one function at a time from a figure who embodies it. Perhaps a therapist or your grandmother really cared for you. Perhaps your teacher at some age was a great guide. Maybe an older sibling protected you well. And there’s always your future healed self if you can imagine that.
For warmth, think of someone you remember fondly. How would they sit beside your little one? Just make sure it’s someone who liked you the way you were.
For protecting, ask what a minimally competent adult would do here. Maybe something simple, like actually smelling that old food you’re about to eat and then trashing it if it smells a little weird. If you’re about to send an angry text, hit pause. If the room itself triggers your spidey sense, leave, or lock the door and get help. Even if this still feels like the child acting like the adult, for now, that’s ok. “Fake it til you make it” isn’t exactly it, but yeah. Afterward, you can tell your little one, “I did that for us. That was the Protector.” If it sounds funny, laugh!
The Guide can be you too, just a calmer you. That’s a lot easier to imagine than your future healed self. Think back to what (and how) you decided about something like this the last time you were calm. Or ask what the wise person you respect would have you practice today. A wise tradition (like “What would Jesus do?” or “What would Buddha do?”) can give some direction, too, until you develop your own internal compass.

original: Sometimes you have a really good session where you feel how much you care about your little one and say what they needed to hear. A few days later you’re skipping lunch and saying yes to everything again. For a lot of people, the first thought is that they didn’t go deep enough. I doubt that’s the problem, and the session doesn’t sound like a failure to me. Try a tiny bit of what you did for your little one as you go about your day, because one small thing like that can teach them more than ten more good meditations. Text a friend that you’re having a rough day instead of saying you’re fine, for instance. Sending that text can be harder than the meditation was.

original: The closest comparison that’s worth mentioning is the out-of-body perception in some near-death experiences. People sometimes report seeing things from impossible angles, and a controversial subset of those reports were verified by others in the room. Those cases had a target that other people could check, and my room experience didn’t, since I wasn’t floating around noticing specific details. So they can’t vouch for my event, but they help show what I mean by an experience that wasn’t stuck at the body’s vantage point anymore. If you want to dig in, there’s this systematic analysis of near-death reports, the AWARE-II cardiac-arrest study, and a recent veridical-NDE evidence scale.

original: I think most people who chase spiritual freedom are also trying to get away from something painful in themselves, and a lot of it goes back to childhood. That’s spiritual bypassing. Plenty of seekers and gurus do it too; I’ve written about the Dalai Lama as one example. I did it too. It doesn’t mean you’re stupid or crazy.

original: For many people, healing does get around to some forgiveness eventually, or at least to not being run by the resentment anymore. It can’t be put on a schedule. And you don’t have to forgive first to get safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice or get better. Then again, active resentment narrows what you see, and your little one stays organized around the injury. And if someone pressures you into forgiving early, what you get is an enlightened-looking act, with the wound gone underground.
rewrite: For many people, healing does get around to some forgiveness eventually, or at least to not being run by the resentment anymore. It can’t be put on a schedule. And no, you don’t have to forgive first to get safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice or get better. Then again, when you’re actively resentful you get tunnel vision, and your little one’s world keeps revolving around the injury. And if someone pressures you into forgiving early, you end up with an enlightened-looking act, while the wound goes underground.

original: If you ever want to retire the shortcut, stop practicing it, take it out of your recordings and any apps that play it, and go back to your usual induction. Decide that while you’re wide awake, and tell yourself so. Don’t be surprised if it still works on you for a while, though, since saying it’s gone doesn’t erase it overnight. You can also keep it, but only to start a session you’ve chosen ahead of time. If it keeps pulling you in when you don’t want it to, or you come out of it disoriented, find someone qualified to help you with it, like a therapist who knows hypnosis.

original:
One more thing about telling whether it helped. A few hours of feeling lighter, with the old feeling back the same day, is a few hours of relief. I’d take that! I just wouldn’t call the problem solved from it, or give the exercise all the credit, especially if you also slept well for once. Jot down what changed and how long it lasted if you want, and then leave it alone.
How many tries is enough? I really don’t know, and I’d be suspicious of anyone who promises you a number, including you, since some things shift in a day and some take about as long as learning guitar. If it’s making things worse, or you just can’t do it right now, I’d change course sooner (stopping counts). Not wanting to do it anymore is a reason too, but if that “nope” sounds like a part of you that’s trying to protect you, I’d hear it out first. If it still says no, that’s your answer. And if you keep following the reparenting steps correctly without getting the expected results, consider if you have a unique case these steps don’t match yet. Maybe you’ll find something that works better for you, or you can ask me what I’d do for this case, or ask a therapist you work with. Either way, I’d like to hear about it!

original:
If the Love Isn’t Coming Yet
If you weren’t loved well as a child, “love your inner child” can sound like nonsense. Love them how? Maybe you really want the best for your little one. Maybe you hug them in your imagination, or miss them. And you can still feel none of the warmth people mean when they say love. That doesn’t close the door, though, it just means you start smaller.
Maybe just imagining a caring grown-up makes you feel more threatened, or lonelier. Lonelier is a strange one, with somebody right there. Then go smaller still, to the least cruel response a decent adult could offer your little one. It’s scaffolding, and it isn’t a test of whether you were loved enough.
Taking the hostility out makes room for warmth. What people most often say helped is letting their defenses down. I mean by choice, after the part guarding you has been heard. If you’ve never been safe being loved, your ego can act like a rigid security guard that won’t let the feeling in, and being vulnerable is the opening the feeling needs. (This guard is only about letting the feeling in. People still have to earn your trust.) Sometimes the warmth is there, with a cold part standing in front of it, guarding something. That part tends to step aside once it’s been heard (see the section Hear the Guard First).
If the love still isn’t coming, you can at least stop judging your little one. Obviously no insults. Helpful advice is great, we all need advice. Let them absorb it at their pace. And don’t expect a thank-you for the session, like they booked it. That’s enough to start being the adult, even if it isn’t enough yet for them to trust you. That takes warmth, and if there isn’t any yet, borrow some.
Your little one might not take it well at first. 😜 More like “Oh, so NOW you care?” Your first instinct might be “But I’m trying!” Some days, just hearing it out like a decent adult is the only thing you’ll manage to borrow.

original:
Some families run on a bargain like “If I’m happy while someone I love is suffering, I’m abandoning them.”
That’s exactly why I was crying for 14 years. Beginning at the age of 12, when I really started to understand that life is brutal for most people, I became convinced that being happy myself, while others weren’t, was selfish. I had this poster in my room that really resonated with me, by the famous socialist, Eugene V. Debs. I told this to a therapist in college and she actually agreed it was a good reason to be depressed!
What I found, once I started cultivating my own happiness, was that I got a lot better at helping other people toward theirs. That might not be how it goes for everyone, and it doesn’t mean unhappy people can’t help. Do your part for people who are suffering, and skip the part where you have to be miserable too.
Some friends or family really might not like it when you get happier, though. Someone might pull away, or keep dragging you back into the old misery. I’d take that loss seriously, and look at what they do and what you owe them, before deciding it’s envy.
I’d still try a small good thing, like a nice meal, and see what actually happens.

original:
The 15-minute daily practice
You don't need to learn a second script for this. It's the same process (gather your attention, notice what's here, respond, wait, and come all the way back), just for fifteen minutes or so. That is long enough to induce yourself (it only takes a few minutes), practice and let it unfold at its own pace, and come out again (that takes a few minutes too). Fifteen minutes is just a handy appointment with yourself, though, and your feelings don't have to keep to it. Five minutes is plenty to see what happens when you simply sit in silence, listening, and you can interrupt yourself at any time to change direction if that feels better.
You can also try other ways of inducing yourself, such as becoming aware of 3 things you can see, 3 things you can hear, 3 things you can feel in your body; then 2 of each, 1 of each. Then count from 5 to 1 and begin to listen. Choose one way to induce yourself. You don't need to try all of them (in fact, stacking them might be counter-productive).
Once you have practiced listening a few times with the recordings, you may want to shorten them to speed up your induction, or even practice without playing them back at all. On the other hand, if you like using the recordings, there is no reason to stop. (Once you know the induction well, the cue from "A shortcut back into hypnosis" can shorten it too.)
As you come out of the process, ask yourself what needed warmth, what needed to be protected, what you need to do differently to be more in accord with truth and love and life. Is there something you want to explore more fully or a capacity you want to build? And most importantly, what can you now carry yourself that you used to have to borrow? If you identified something you needed to do differently, make a plan with yourself to do that thing. The more specific you can be, the more likely you are to change: “If _________ (fill in the cue for the old pattern), then I will do ________ (fill in a small action that will begin to change the pattern).” Then check back later and see how you are doing – sleeping, relating, functioning, etc., not only how impressive the session felt.

original: Part of building who you are is untangling yourself from whatever pulls you away from your own knowing in return for belonging. A political tribe might expect consistent positions and predictable reactions, while a family or religion that’s kind to you might have expectations that just feel like being good. Most groups expect some conformity, which is ordinary. Your family might want a particular kind of son or daughter, and your friends might have rules about what you can joke about or get upset about. But if going along means betraying yourself, that’s the bargain. It can help to write down the rules your family ran on, including unspoken ones like “Boys don’t cry.” Then write down the role you got handed, like the stand-in parent, or the one who got blamed for everything (ST-CA has lists of both, in sections 15.2.3 and 15.2.4).

original: What’s starving them is anomie. We evolved to live in small groups where everybody knows, loves, and trusts everybody. In a large society, the shared norms and close ties that held those groups together fall apart. Nobody knows anybody well enough, or for long enough, to tell who can be trusted. Even your next-door neighbor is often a total stranger. That’s how large societies end up run by psychopaths. (Yes, I’m always going on about this.)
rewrite: What’s starving them is anomie. What’s anomie? Well, we evolved to live in small groups where everybody knows everybody, and they love and trust each other. In a large society, the shared norms and close ties that held those groups together fall apart. Nobody knows anybody well enough, or for long enough, to tell who can be trusted. Even your next-door neighbor is often a total stranger. That’s how large societies end up run by psychopaths. (Yes, I’m always going on about this.)

So inner child therapy draws on those higher vantage points more concretely. The inner Guide is the closest thing here to a Higher Self, and it has to work with the Nurturer and Protector and come after them. It can’t act like some transcendent authority that waves everything away. Most reparenting doesn’t do enough with the Guide, which is the opposite extreme from IFS, so I’m trying to bring together the best of both. IFS isn’t exactly one system, so I may be simplifying it here. It has its own branches and disputes, and that’s one more problem I’m trying to remedy by laying all this out systematically in this guide.
IFS calls these wounded young parts “exiles.” I find that pathologizing. I prefer to speak of a child who needs parenting and integration, rather than naming them by their wounded or excluded condition.
And the parts just keep coming: managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts... At some point it’s a maze, with a little one somewhere in the middle of it. Some practitioners are gentle about it and walk you through the maze just fine. Others seem to leave people more split up than when they started. A big institute and a pile of certificates won’t tell you whether a model is true, or whether it’s safe for you.

original: Science only gets to circle the edges of consciousness, though it finds some wild stuff out there: people functioning with no felt controller, several things cognized at once, split-brain patients who can seem like two knowers sharing a skull, and one recent theory that models minds as nested parallel observers. The full nerdy tour is in the research report. Science gives my argument a third wheel, making it safer to ride, but it will never show nibbāna itself – self and sense organs unweaving into self-presenting light flows of bliss. That requires meditation.

original:
When the Practice Feels Real but Stays Shallow
Some people have the opposite problem. It feels like you’re connecting with your little one, but the contact is staying near the surface. Meditating for a long time and then sleeping can open up much more emotionally direct stuff, especially in a second sleep, after you’ve already slept once. What showed me that the daytime pl/ork had stayed shallow was the difference at night. Say you wake up from a dream soaked in way more feeling and need than anything the session got near. Then this is probably you. A nice session that just wears off is a different thing. I’d ask what the dream let you feel that the session didn’t, and look at it again after your morning coffee. And if nightmares start wrecking your sleep, dial the practice down by doing it earlier in the day, or for less time.

original:
Forgiveness without bypass
We cannot force forgiveness on ourselves. It has to come from a place of understanding, otherwise it can be bypassing. However, if we remain in the anger forever, we are allowing the injury to dictate how we live our lives in the present. So how do we hold all of this? We just remember that it can all be true at once. They really did hurt us and they still have to answer for it. Our boundary with them is crucial to maintain, especially after forgiveness which can tend to weaken it. One day we may find that we have forgiven them for not knowing better, just like Jesus did on the Cross.
You might say to the part of you that got hurt, “I’m not going to use spiritual mumbo jumbo to shush your cries and make you forgive before you're ready. But I’m also not going to build our whole life around this wound forever.”
Forgiving yourself
For self-forgiveness, name what you regret doing, and take responsibility for just that part. Let yourself feel the remorse by taking in the harm done. See how it went against your values. Stop short of making yourself a permanent criminal by identifying with the behaviors you're now abandoning.
Do what you can to put it right. Every so often, come back to how you got to be someone who could do that, until you understand the pattern well enough that it can't drive you anymore.

original: The closest thing I can compare it to is the out-of-body part of some near-death experiences. People sometimes report seeing things from impossible angles, and some of those reports (controversially) were verified by others in the room. My room event had nothing like that to check, though, since I wasn’t floating around noticing any details. So those cases can’t back mine up. They just help me show what I mean by an experience that wasn’t stuck at the body’s vantage point anymore. If you want to go down that rabbit hole, there’s this systematic analysis of near-death reports, the AWARE-II cardiac-arrest study, and a recent veridical-NDE evidence scale.

original: Milder reactions afterward count as caution signs too, like getting confused or spaced out (dissociating) again and again. Get professional help right away if any of this is severe or risky, and especially if it keeps going or comes back while you’re sober. Don’t suddenly quit a prescribed medicine, or anything your body is dependent on, just because it might be part of the problem; have a doctor help you stop safely.

original:
Once you’ve got your bearings, make your first wish.
"Please show me the next truth. The next symbol or feeling. The question or action that's useful for me at this time, and no more than I can handle."
Stay awake when your mind likes to escape
If your mind keeps drifting off, sit up and open your eyes. Then feel your feet on the floor, and just let your breathing go at its own pace. Tell yourself, "I'm not going anywhere. I'm happily arriving more fully here each moment."
Pick something in the room to look at, and feel your spine at the same time (focusing on two things makes it harder for the mind to use multitasking mode to wander). Then ask yourself what the daydreaming is doing for you. Is it bringing you guidance? Does it help you work through a feeling, or are you using it to avoid something?
Ask for any diffuse benefits to become more practically focused: "If this is guidance, show me what I need to do about it. If I'm avoiding something, bring me gently back to the present and show me what it is."
Make the hypnosis more alert
Aside from focusing on things in your direct experience, you can also suggest yourself into greater alertness (it's still relaxed-alert, not paranoid-alert). Keep your eyes open. Use a small hand movement each time you make the auto-suggestion that you're gaining increasing clarity. Then stop the hand movement and see where your mind is at. That hand movement is the mental escape into the body's flow. Say something like,
“Starting with your eyes open, press your thumb to your forefinger, gently, and let go. As you do, you begin to bring yourself into a place of clearer awareness… Press and let go again, and you’re clearer still. And once more, into the clearest state of awareness yet. Now stop pressing. In the first second after you stop, notice if there’s any echo of the pressing in your fingers, in your breathing, in your attention, or nowhere at all. Just notice, sit up straight and work from this level.”
